Rumors in social systems are omnipresent. While traditional models focus on pairwise interactions,
the collective effects of group interactions are insufﬁciently explored. Here we present a rumor
propagation model on higher-order networks that incorporates 2-simplex structures and adaptive
transitions between active and passive individuals. We ﬁnd that higher-order networks substantially
lower the propagation threshold and intensify nonlinear spreading effects. Active individuals are key
drivers of rumor propagation and persistence. With active contagion, we observe that higher-order
propagation increases peak and steady-state densities of active spreaders, thus extending the
propagation and lifespan of rumors. We also apply a sequential quadratic programming algorithm to
optimize the parameters of our model and validate its accuracy and applicability on real-world data.
These results advance our understanding of contagion in higher-order social networks and support
the design of targeted strategies for rumor mitigation.
Rumor propagation has been a topic of sustained scholarly interest due to
its profound impact on societal dynamics, decision-making processes,
and the shaping of public opinion. In recent years, the proliferation of
online social networks has dramatically accelerated the speed and scale of
rumor propagation, prompting the need to understand and control these
processes1–3. Traditional rumor propagation models, which primarily
focus on pairwise interactions, have provided valuable insights, but they
fall short in representing the complexity of real-world networks, in
particular the group dynamics contained within such networks. Higher-
order interactions that can link together multiple individuals at once
serve as much better means of modeling critical mechanisms that are
involved in rumor propagation and activity contagion. Such group
interactions drive key phenomena such as the conformity effect4–6, peer
inﬂuence7–9, social reinforcement10–13, and the Goebbels effect14,15, all of
which are essential to understand the dynamics of rumor propagation
and activity contagion in realistic social networks.
Indeed, research in recent years has shown that higher-order net-
works provide a versatile framework for studying the dynamics of com-
plex systems, extending the traditional pairwise interaction paradigm to

spreading, activity contagion involves the adoption of behaviors within
groups, where collective dynamics play a critical role. Individual activity
states are simultaneously inﬂuenced by those around them. A pioneering
effort is the simplicial activity-driven model proposed by Petri and Barrat,
which incorporates group interactions into time-varying networks and
simulates contagion dynamics within higher-order structures26. Their work
highlights how activity and higher-order topology together shape the evo-
lution of SIS-like spreading processes, emphasizing the importance of
modeling beyond pairwise interactions. Along similar lines, other studies
have also emphasized the importance of activity in shaping rumor
dynamics27–29. For instance, Rizzo et al. developed a susceptible-infected-
susceptible model based on activity-driven networks, demonstrating that
behavioral changes can mitigate disease transmission by increasing the
epidemic threshold and decreasing the steady-state fraction of infected
individuals30. Moreover, Cheng et al. expanded on this concept by incor-
porating ﬂuctuations in activity within a stochastic version of the rumor
model31. And Zeng et al. examined the correlation between activity and
attractiveness, elucidating its impacts on both epidemic spreading and
rumor diffusion32.
However, research thus far has not focused on utilizing simpli-
cial complexes to model rumor propagation. Furthermore, studies
addressing individual activity seldom consider the contagion of
activity states. In the context of rumor propagation dynamics, this
phenomenon describes how individuals transition between active and
passive states due to group interactions. Systematically incorporating
activity contagion into rumor propagation models thus enables a
deeper understanding of how rumors gain momentum, transition
between individuals with different activity states, and eventually
saturate or dissipate within a network. Finally, the interplay between
interaction and coevolution further enriches our understanding of
rumor dynamics. Interaction processes, including active or passive
contagion and higher-order propagation, evolve dynamically in
response to changes in the states of network nodes. This coevolu-
tionary nature underscores the necessity for adaptive models that can
capture the many feedback loops between network structure, indi-
vidual behavior, and the progression of rumor dynamics.
Based on these observations and proceeding research, our con-
tribution in this paper are ﬁve-fold. In the ﬁrst place, we propose an
adaptive rumor propagation model that integrates higher-order propa-
gation mechanisms with activity contagion processes within an adaptive
network framework. By incorporating both pairwise interactions and 2-
simplex-based group interactions, the model offers an integrated view of
the propagation, evolution, and stabilization of rumors in adaptive net-
works. Secondly, to address the dynamic nature of individual activity
levels in social networks and their dependence on neighboring inﬂuences,
we present the framework of an activity contagion 2-simplex to describe
both active and passive contagion processes. Serving as a modeling tool,
this approach provides a robust theoretical foundation for understanding
rumor dynamics. Thirdly, we examine the intricate coupling effects
between activity contagion processes and higher-order propagation
structures. The analysis offers key insights into the nonlinear behavior of
rumor propagation in modern information ecosystems and highlights
practical strategies for rumor suppression. Fourthly, through large-scale
simulation experiments, we reveal the bifurcation characteristics of the
system under varying parameter conditions. Critical thresholds are
identiﬁed for key parameters, including the higher-order propagation
probability, active contagion probability, and the average degree of
higher-order structures. Furthermore, the results uncover nonlinear
characteristics induced by higher-order propagation mechanisms, which
emerge through steady-state transitions of the system. And ﬁnally, we use
the Sequential Quadratic Programming (SQP) algorithm to identify
optimal model parameters and test its effectiveness and accuracy on real-
world datasets, thus demonstrating its applicability and reliability in
practical rumor propagation research.
Results
Mathematical model
As noted, rumor propagation often exhibits higher-order characteristics,
relying not only on pairwise interactions but also on complex group-level
interactions. In this context, traditional rumor propagation models struggle
to adequately capture the higher-order diffusion dynamics of rumors in
complex networks. At the same time, individuals exhibit differences in their
activity levels, distinguishing them as active or passive. Active individuals
prefer to initiate communication, while passive individuals wait to be
engaged by active users. Individuals with different activity states occupy
distinct roles within the rumor propagation process. However, an indivi-
dual’s activity state is not static, it evolves through interactions with sur-
rounding individuals. This phenomenon, referred to as activity contagion,
signiﬁcantly inﬂuences propagation dynamics, representing a self-adaptive
property of the system that is often overlooked in traditional models.
To address this gap, this paper proposes an adaptive higher-order
rumor propagation model incorporating activity contagion, with the goal of
accurately capturing both the diffusion dynamics of rumors in complex
networks and the system’s adaptive processes. The model is schematically
illustrated in Fig. 1.
The model incorporates multiple propagation mechanisms, such as
pairwise interaction propagation and n-simplex-based propagation, to
capture the heterogeneous propagation pathways and inﬂuence scales
observedinreal-worldnetworks.Foranalyticalclarity,thisstudyspeciﬁcally
focuses on pairwise interaction propagation and 2-simplex-based propa-
gation. Additionally, across the various types of 2-simplices involved in
rumor propagation, both active and passive contagion may take place,
governed by the activity states of the individuals. Figure 1(a) illustrates the
schematic diagram of individual interaction propagation, Fig. 1(b) depicts
the 2-simplex-based rumor propagation process, and Fig. 1(c) presents the
2-simplex-based activity contagion process. All these processes are assumed
to occur within a virtual community, where individuals dynamically enter
and exit. Speciﬁcally, active and passive individuals enter the community at
rates Λa and Λp, respectively, while all individuals leave the community at a
uniform rate μ. Within the community, rumor-forgetting also occurs. The
parameter δ represents the probability of forgetting the rumor. The para-
meter deﬁnitions are summarized in Table 1, and the detailed analysis is
provided below.
(1) Rumor propagation rules.
Rumor propagation occurs through two main modes: pairwise pro-
pagation and 2-simplex propagation. The speciﬁc propagation rules are as
follows:
1) Pairwise propagation.
The speciﬁc rules for pairwise propagation are as follows:
When an active ignorant (Ia) contacts an active spreader (Sa), it tran-
sitions to Sa with a probability of β1.
When an active ignorant (Ia) contacts a passive spreader (Sp), Ia con-
verts to Sa with a probability of β2.
When a passive ignorant (Ip) contacts an active spreader (Sa), Ip con-
verts to Sp with a probability of β3.
Since both Ip and Sp are passive, they do not initiate communication.
Therefore, rumors cannot propagate between these two individuals.
Activeindividualsaremoreinclinedtoparticipateinpropagation,such
that β1 > β2 > β3. Passive individuals (Ip and Sp) do not actively engage in
propagation unless contacted by an active individual. Consequently, the
propagation dynamics within the network are inﬂuenced by the number of
active nodes and the states of their neighbors. The average degree of the
1-simplex is denoted by 〈k〉.
2) 2-Simplex propagation.
2-simplex propagation refers to group-level rumor propagation, where
a group of three nodes jointly participates in the propagation process. For
analytical simplicity, this study focuses solely on groups composed of three
nodes. In this mode, rumors can spread rapidly within a triad, such as a
group consisting of Ia-Sa-Sa, as illustrated in Fig. 1(b). The speciﬁc propa-

(2) Activity contagion rules.
During the activity contagion process, once a rumor propagation
2-simplex is activated, if any one of the nodes in the triad is in a different
activity state than the other two neighbors, the individual will be inﬂuenced
to change its activity state (node’s self-adaptation). In this case, the activity
contagion 2-simplex is triggered, as shown by the green triangle in Fig. 1(c).
Speciﬁcally,
When nodes in a triad consist of Ia, Sa, and Sa, the activity contagion
2-simplex is not triggered because all the nodes are active individuals.
When nodes in a triad consist of Ia, Sp, and Sa, the activity contagion
2-simplex is triggered, and Sp is inﬂuenced by its neighbors, transitioning to
an active state with probability γ1.
When nodes in a triad consist of Ia, Sp, and Sp, the activity contagion
2-simplex is triggered, and Ia is inﬂuenced by its neighbors, transitioning to
an inactive state with probability ω.
When nodes in a triad consist of Ip, Sa, and Sa, the activity contagion
2-simplex is triggered, and Ip is inﬂuenced by its neighbors, transitioning to
an active state with probability γ2.
When nodes in a triad consist of Ip, Sp, and Sa, the activity contagion
2-simplex is not triggered because the rumor propagation 2-simplex is not
activated.
When nodes in a triad consist of Ip, Sp, and Sp, the activity contagion
2-simplex is not triggered because all the nodes are passive individuals.
The activity contagion process further inﬂuences the rumor propa-
gation process, forming an interactive co-evolutionary process.

on the dynamics of rumor propagation. Figure 2(a)–(c) illustrate that when

rumor-prevalent equilibrium, marked by widespread and persistent rumor
diffusion, accompanied by substantial increases in the densities of both
active and passive spreaders. This suggests the presence of a bifurcation

meter variations with γ1 in the critical range of [0.6, 0.7], demonstrating
abrupt transitions from a rumor-free equilibrium to a rumor-prevalent
equilibrium. This abrupt state change emphasizes the system’s nonlinear
nature, suggesting that small changes in parameters near the critical
threshold can trigger substantial shifts in system behavior.

that as γ1 increases, the intensity and efﬁciency of individual interactions

spreaders into active spreaders, thereby amplifying the prevalence of
rumors. In Fig. 2(b), the density of passive spreaders (Sp) follows a non-

breaks and diffusion. Furthermore, implementing tailored control strategies

Discussion
In this study, we have introduced an adaptive rumor propagation model
built on higher-order networks and active contagion mechanisms. We have
revealed the nonlinear interactions between higher-order propagation
structures, activity contagion probability, and pairwise propagation prob-
ability, emphasizing their crucial impact on the dynamics of rumor pro-
pagation. Through theoretical analysis and numerical simulations, we have
highlighted several important ﬁndings.
Higher-order propagation structures, such as 2-simplex and 3-simplex
formations, have signiﬁcantly lowered the threshold for the initiation of
rumorpropagation.Thiseffecthasbecomemorepronouncedastheaverage
degree of higher-order structures has increased. We have suggested that
controlling the formation and density of higher-order structures within a
network can delay the start of rumor propagation and slow its initial
momentum. Additionally, we have observed that the interplay between
pairwise and higher-order propagation mechanisms indicates that higher-
order structures dominate when pairwise propagation is weak. In contrast,
their inﬂuence diminishes as pairwise propagation intensiﬁes. We have
concluded that effective management must therefore address both pairwise
and higher-order spreading paths to mitigate overall propagation.
Activecontagionhasplayedakeyroleinamplifyingboththespeedand
scaleofrumorspread.Highlyactivenodes,suchaskeyopinionleaders,have
acted as pivotal drivers of propagation. Targeted strategies, such as identi-
fying and intervening with these nodes, have proven effective in limiting the
ampliﬁcation effect and decelerating rumor dissemination. We have also
shown that the critical threshold for higher-order propagation adjusts
dynamically with changes in network complexity and node activity. We
have recommended real-time monitoring and preemptive interventions to
reduce network density or node activity to help prevent rumors from
reaching their propagation threshold.
However, while we propose intervention strategies such as reducing
propagation probabilities and increasing individual activity thresholds
based on sensitivity analyses, this study does not explicitly simulate or
empirically validate these measures. Our focus has been on uncovering the
core propagation dynamics driven by higher-order structures and activity
contagion. We acknowledge that controlled experiments or real-world case
studies would further substantiate the effectiveness of such interventions,
and we identify this as a promising direction for future work.
The validity of our model has been conﬁrmed through comparisons
with real-world data, demonstrating its ability to accurately replicate the
dynamics of rumor propagation in early stages. This suggests its potential as
a practical tool for analyzing and managing rumor spread in real-world
networks.
While this study primarily focuses on three-node interactions (i.e.,
2-simplex structures), the modeling framework could, in principle, be
extended to capture more complex higher-order group interactions. These
extensionsmayuncoverrichercollectivebehaviors.However,incorporating
such higher-dimensional structures introduces additional modeling and
computational challenges, including increased runtime costs and potential
ambiguity in inﬂuence direction—particularly in even-sized groups. Future
studiescouldexploreappropriateassumptionsorvoting-basedmechanisms
to resolve such ambiguities and assess whether qualitative changes emerge
in higher-order extensions. Moreover, even under the current model, the
inclusion of higher-order interactions and dynamic adaptation already
increases computational complexity, which may limit scalability in large or
noisy real-world networks. Future work could explore approximation
techniques, reduced-order models, or algorithmic optimizations to improve
computational efﬁciency and enhance real-time applicability.
In addressing these computational challenges, emerging methods
such as Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) may offer a pro-
mising direction37. By embedding domain-speciﬁc knowledge into neural
network training, PINNs can potentially improve the predictive perfor-
mance and learning efﬁciency of rumor dynamics models. Moreover,
PINNs may aid in optimizing intervention strategies through data-driven
control mechanisms.
Beyond rumor propagation, the modeling framework presented here
has broader potential applications, including misinformation diffusion,
crisis communication, and marketing campaigns. Validating the model
across diverse scenarios and datasets could further demonstrate its gen-
eralizability and provide insights into the spread of various types of infor-
mation in complex social systems.
These insights can inform strategies for managing not only rumors but
also the spread of misinformation, marketing campaigns, or public health
messages in interconnected systems. Furthermore, the dynamic adjustment
of thresholds has underscored the need for adaptive and proactive inter-
ventions that account for the evolving nature of network complexity. We
have laid a foundation for future research into higher-order network
dynamics, offering new avenues for tackling challenges in ﬁelds such as
social media governance, public communication, and network-based
decision-making.
